Period schedule:

Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

section_titles: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
periods.activity_title: Grids, Kits, and the Same Whole

tasks_in_class.description: Shade 1/8 of Grid A in red, 1/6 of Grid B in blue, 1/12 of Grid C in yellow; mark 1/3 in any grid.
In groups of 3–4, find different ways to make a whole with different fraction pieces; write equivalent fractions for 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6.
Using kit or shading, find how many 1/12s make 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6.

time_bands.activity: Open with the chocolate puzzle from the chapter: can 1/3 of one chocolate be bigger than 1/2 of another? Children discuss in pairs and share answers. Bring out the idea that the size of the whole determines the size of the fraction — no formal rule yet, just voiced intuitions.

Distribute the three grids. Children work through Playing with a Grid, p.17 ("Shade 1/8 of Grid A in red, 1/6 of Grid B in blue, 1/12 of Grid C in yellow; mark 1/3 in any grid...."). Pairs compare their shaded regions and notice that 1/3 looks different across different-sized grids.

Distribute fraction kit pieces. Groups build a whole using different-sized pieces and record findings for Let Us Do Q1, p.19 ("In groups of 3–4, find different ways to make a whole...."). Then groups tackle Let Us Do Q2C(a)–(d), p.19 ("Using kit or shading, find how many 1/12s make 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6."), fitting pieces and writing the equivalent fractions they discover.

periods.teacher_notes: A common confusion is that 1/3 and 1/4 are compared by the numerator alone — children may say '1/3 > 1/4 because 3 > 4'; use the kit pieces to show that each 1/3 piece is physically larger than each 1/4 piece. Additional practice on how many 1/8s make 1/4 and 1/2 is available at Let Us Do Q2A and Q2B(a)–(b), p.19, and the mixed-piece whole-building challenge is at Let Us Do Q3, p.20.
materials: Printed grid sheets (three grids of different sizes per child)
Fraction kit pieces per group (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8, 1/12 pieces)

tasks_in_class.description: Put a tick against pairs that are equivalent: 2/3 & 3/4; 3/5 & 6/10; 4/12 & 2/6; 6/9 & 1/3.
Fill boxes to make equivalent fractions: 2/5 = ?/10; 3/4 = ?/16; 4/7 = 8/?; 5/9 = ?/25.
Compare fractions with same denominator using < and >: 1/4 & 3/4; 3/5 & 4/5; 5/7 & 2/7; 7/8 & 3/8; 5/10 & 6/10; 2/6 & 1/6.

time_bands.activity: Draw a rectangle on the board divided into 3 equal parts; shade one part (1/3). Ask: if I divide each part into 2 again, how many parts do I have? Shade the same region and label it 2/6. Repeat for 3/9. Students observe that the shaded area never changes — only the name of the fraction does. This builds the multiplicative pattern from concrete dividing of figures, as introduced in the making equivalent fractions section.

Children work independently on Let Us Do Q2, p.22 ("Put a tick against pairs that are equivalent: 2/3 & 3/4; 3/5 & 6/10; 4/12 & 2/6; 6/9 & 1/3."), then share reasoning aloud. Follow immediately with Let Us Do Q3, p.22 ("Fill boxes to make equivalent fractions: 2/5 = ?/10; 3/4 = ?/16; 4/7 = 8/?; 5/9 = ?/25.") applying the multiply-numerator-and-denominator-by-the-same-number pattern.

Introduce the chikki-sharing story: Sevi ate 1/3 of a chikki bar and Shami ate 2/3 of the same bar — who ate more? Children reason from the picture and the denominators being the same. Children then work through Let Us Do Q1, p.23 ("Compare fractions with same denominator using < and >: 1/4 & 3/4; 3/5 & 4/5; 5/7 & 2/7; 7/8 & 3/8; 5/10 & 6/10; 2/6 & 1/6."), writing < or > for each pair.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is multiplying only the numerator (writing 1/3 = 2/3 instead of 2/6); drawing the division lines on the figure shows why both numerator and denominator change together. The equivalent-fractions filling task Let Us Do Q1, p.22 (chains for 1/7, 2/3, 3/4, 3/5) provides additional practice and can be set as extension work.

periods.activity_title: Same Pieces, Different Sizes — and Beyond One Whole

tasks_in_class.description: Compare fractions with same numerator using < and >: 3/8 & 3/7; 4/9 & 4/10; 2/7 & 2/5; 5/7 & 5/6; 6/9 & 6/10; 7/9 & 7/11.
Use parathas and number lines in notebook to show 2/3 & 5/3; 3/4 & 5/4; 4/8 & 9/8.
Circle fractions greater than 1 from the given set; discuss reasoning in class.

time_bands.activity: Open with the paratha story: Renu ate 4/6 of a paratha and Meena ate 4/5 of a paratha — same number of pieces, but the paratha was divided differently. Use the fraction-kit circles (fifths and sixths) to show that each 1/6 piece is smaller than each 1/5 piece, so 4/6 < 4/5. Children work through Let Us Do Q1, p.23 ("Compare fractions with same numerator using < and >: 3/8 & 3/7; 4/9 & 4/10; 2/7 & 2/5; 5/7 & 5/6; 6/9 & 6/10; 7/9 & 7/11."), then one child states the generalisation: bigger denominator → smaller fraction when numerators match.

Draw 5 half-paratha images on the board and ask: how many halves are there altogether? Count: 1/2, 2/2, 3/2, 4/2, 5/2 — the class lands on 5/2 > 1. Children then draw parathas and number lines in their notebooks for Let Us Do Q1, p.28 ("Use parathas and number lines in notebook to show 2/3 & 5/3; 3/4 & 5/4; 4/8 & 9/8."), marking each fraction as a point on the line.

Children examine the full set of fractions in Let Us Do Q2, p.28 ("Circle fractions greater than 1 from the given set; discuss reasoning in class."). Pairs first circle their answers, then share the quick test they used — numerator greater than denominator means the fraction exceeds 1. Class consolidates the rule through voiced discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: For same-numerator comparisons, children often (incorrectly) pick the fraction with the larger denominator as the larger fraction, mirroring the same-denominator rule; the fraction-kit circles make the reversal concrete. When introducing fractions greater than 1, note that some children may write 5/2 as five separate fractions rather than one fraction — the number line draws all five halves as steps along a single line and corrects this.

tasks_in_class.description: Circle fractions equal to 1/2 from the given set: 2/4, 3/5, 5/7, 7/14, 5/10, 8/16, 5/9, 6/12, 10/20, 6/8.

time_bands.activity: Write the pair 7/8 and 8/6 on the board. Ask: without common denominators, how can we tell which is bigger? Guide children to check each fraction against 1: 7/8 has numerator less than denominator so it is less than 1; 8/6 has numerator greater than denominator so it exceeds 1 — done. Children apply this benchmark strategy to Let Us Do Q1, p.29 ("Compare fractions using 1 as reference: 8/7 & 9/15; 13/20 & 17/15; 7/6 & 8/8; 6/6 & 19/12; 12/9 & 4/5; 15/5 & 16/4.") and explain each decision orally.

Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and mark 1/2 in the centre. Ask: which fractions sit exactly here? Build up the equivalents: 2/4, 5/10, 6/12. Children then circle fractions equal to 1/2 in Let Us Do Q1, p.30 ("Circle fractions equal to 1/2 from the given set: 2/4, 3/5, 5/7, 7/14, 5/10, 8/16, 5/9, 6/12, 10/20, 6/8."), testing each by asking whether doubling the numerator gives the denominator.

Children work through Let Us Do Q3, p.31 ("Compare 8 fraction pairs using 1/2 as reference: 2/9 & 4/7; 11/14 & 7/20; 5/7 & 3/9; 6/7 & 4/10; 9/17 & 3/15; 7/12 & 3/11; 1/3 & 5/9; 3/9 & 4/7.") by first sorting each fraction as above-half or below-half, then comparing the two. Pairs check each other's answers and discuss any disagreements.

periods.teacher_notes: A common slip when using the 1/2 benchmark is comparing 5/9 with 1/2 and concluding they are equal because both numerator and denominator are odd — remind children the test is whether 2 × numerator equals denominator. Let Us Do Q2, p.30 (circle fractions less than half) provides additional practice for children who need more work before the paired comparison task.

tasks_in_class.description: If an ant is 1/4 cm long, find total length of 16 such ants in a line using the number line.

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: write six fraction pairs on the board, two for each benchmark strategy (same denominator, reference to 1, reference to 1/2). Children call out the answer and name the strategy they used. This recaps the three comparison tools built across the chapter without reintroducing their content.

Present Try This, p.31 ("If an ant is 1/4 cm long, find total length of 16 such ants in a line using the number line."). Children draw a number line in their notebooks, mark 0 and place steps of 1/4 cm one ant at a time, counting up: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 = 1, 5/4, … until 16 steps reach 16/4. They write the improper fraction and then the equivalent whole number. Pairs compare number lines and verify.

A short class gallery: pairs share their number lines and answer. Teacher draws a single large number line on the board, inviting children to mark key milestones (1, 2, 3, 4 cm) and label the quarter steps. Children record the completed number line and the answer (16/4 = 4 cm) in neat in their books, finishing the sitting with a fully solved, self-verified problem.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is stopping the number line at 16 tick marks but not grouping the quarters into whole centimetres — draw the grouping arcs (four quarters = one whole) on the board to make the conversion visible. Children who finish quickly can pose a similar problem: how long would a line of 20 ants be if each ant is 1/5 cm long?

items.prompt: Here are two rectangles of different sizes. Shade 1/4 of the smaller rectangle and 1/4 of the larger rectangle. Are the two shaded parts equal in size? Write one sentence explaining your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two shaded parts are not equal in size. Each is 1/4 of its own rectangle, but because the rectangles are different sizes, the shaded regions are different sizes too.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Shade one quarter of each rectangle by dividing it into 4 equal parts and colouring one; compare the shaded areas directly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: let them cut and fold the rectangles to find one quarter physically; stretch: ask what would need to be true for both shaded parts to be equal.

exercise.description: Shade 1/8 of Grid A in red, 1/6 of Grid B in blue, 1/12 of Grid C in yellow; mark 1/3 in any grid.

items.section_title: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
items.prompt: Priya places two 1/6 pieces of her fraction kit end to end. Which fraction do they together make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/3, because two 1/6 pieces fit exactly into one 1/3 piece, showing 2/6 = 1/3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fit two 1/6 pieces against the 1/3 piece; they match exactly, giving the equivalent fraction.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added denominators (6 + 6 = 12) rather than counting how many pieces fill a known fraction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student did not combine the pieces and left the answer as a single piece.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student guessed a nearby unit fraction without using the kit relationship.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: have them physically place two 1/6 pieces against the 1/3 piece from a fraction kit; stretch: ask how many 1/12 pieces would be needed to make the same amount.

exercise.description: In groups of 3–4, find different ways to make a whole with different fraction pieces; write equivalent fractions for 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6.

items.section_title: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
items.prompt: How many 1/12 pieces does it take to fill one 1/4 piece exactly? Write the equivalent fraction this shows.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three 1/12 pieces fill one 1/4 piece exactly. This shows that 3/12 = 1/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place 1/12 pieces one by one onto the 1/4 piece until it is full; count the pieces to read the numerator of the equivalent fraction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: let them use physical fraction kit pieces to fill and count; stretch: ask them to find a second equivalent fraction for 1/4 using a different-sized piece.

exercise.description: Using kit or shading, find how many 1/12s make 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6.

items.prompt: Rajan has 7 quarter-paratha pieces. Draw a number line from 0 to 2 and mark the point that shows 7/4. Then write 7/4 as a mixed number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7/4 is marked one step before 2 on the number line. As a mixed number it is 1 and 3/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count 7 steps of 1/4 from 0 along the number line; after 4 steps you reach 1, so 7 steps land at 1 and 3/4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: have them draw 7 quarter-sized paratha pieces and group 4 into one whole; stretch: ask them to locate 11/4 on the same number line.

exercise.description: Use parathas and number lines in notebook to show 2/3 & 5/3; 3/4 & 5/4; 4/8 & 9/8.

items.prompt: Which pair of fractions is equivalent?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3/5 and 6/10 are equivalent because multiplying both 3 and 5 by 2 gives 6 and 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether numerator and denominator of one fraction can be multiplied by the same whole number to give the other fraction.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have confused numerator growth (2 to 3) with denominator growth (3 to 4) without checking the multiplying factor is the same for both.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have tried to simplify 6/9 by dividing only the numerator, obtaining 2/3, not checking whether 1/3 follows the same rule.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have recognised consecutive numerators and denominators as a pattern without testing the multiplicative relationship.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: have them shade both fractions on identical rectangles and compare; stretch: ask them to write two more fractions equivalent to 3/5.

exercise.description: Put a tick against pairs that are equivalent: 2/3 & 3/4; 3/5 & 6/10; 4/12 & 2/6; 6/9 & 1/3.

items.prompt: Asha ate 5/8 of a roti and Banu ate 5/6 of a roti of the same size. Who ate more? Write one sentence explaining why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Banu ate more. Both ate 5 pieces, but each of Banu's pieces (sixths) is bigger than each of Asha's pieces (eighths) because a roti divided into 6 parts gives larger pieces than one divided into 8 parts.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When numerators are equal, compare denominators — the smaller denominator means larger pieces, so that fraction is greater.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: draw two same-sized circles divided into 8 and 6 equal parts and shade 5 parts of each; stretch: pose a new same-numerator pair and ask the student to explain without drawing.

exercise.description: Compare fractions with same numerator using < and >: 3/8 & 3/7; 4/9 & 4/10; 2/7 & 2/5; 5/7 & 5/6; 6/9 & 6/10; 7/9 & 7/11.

items.prompt: Which of these fractions is greater than 1?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 11/8 is greater than 1 because its numerator (11) is greater than its denominator (8).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fraction exceeds 1 when its numerator is greater than its denominator; check each option by comparing numerator and denominator.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may not have applied the numerator-denominator comparison; 7 < 9 so 7/9 is less than 1.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have confused equal numerator and denominator (which equals exactly 1) with greater than 1.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student selected a fraction clearly less than 1, suggesting the benchmark rule has not been grasped.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: draw a number line from 0 to 2 and ask them to place each fraction; stretch: ask them to write two fractions of their own that are greater than 1 but less than 2.

exercise.description: Circle fractions greater than 1 from the given set; discuss reasoning in class.

items.prompt: Compare 9/10 and 7/5 without finding a common denominator. Which statement is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: 9/10 < 7/5 because 9/10 is less than 1 and 7/5 is greater than 1

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9/10 < 7/5. Since 9 < 10, the fraction 9/10 is less than 1. Since 7 > 5, the fraction 7/5 is greater than 1. Therefore 9/10 is smaller.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each fraction against 1 by comparing its numerator and denominator; the fraction less than 1 is automatically smaller than the fraction greater than 1.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student compared numerators directly (9 vs 7) without checking the size of each fraction relative to 1.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student applied an irrelevant property (odd numerators) instead of the benchmark test.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student compared denominators directly (10 vs 5) without applying the benchmark strategy.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: ask them to place both fractions on a number line and see which is to the left of 1 and which to the right; stretch: give a pair where both fractions exceed 1 and ask whether the same benchmark approach still works.

items.prompt: Which of these fractions is equal to 1/2?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6/12 equals 1/2 because 2 × 6 = 12, so the denominator is exactly double the numerator.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether doubling the numerator gives the denominator exactly; if yes, the fraction equals 1/2.

what_each_option_reveals.B: 4/10 has denominator 10 and numerator 4; doubling 4 gives 8, not 10, so this is less than 1/2; the student may have guessed from the digits.
what_each_option_reveals.C: 5/9 has denominator 9 and numerator 5; doubling 5 gives 10, not 9, so this is slightly more than 1/2; the student may have treated the 1-apart gap as equality.
what_each_option_reveals.A: 3/8 has denominator 8 and numerator 3; doubling 3 gives 6, not 8, so this is less than 1/2; the student may have chosen a fraction that looks like a simple fraction.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: draw a bar divided into 12 equal parts and shade 6, then ask whether exactly half is shaded; stretch: ask the student to write three more fractions equal to 1/2.

exercise.description: Circle fractions equal to 1/2 from the given set: 2/4, 3/5, 5/7, 7/14, 5/10, 8/16, 5/9, 6/12, 10/20, 6/8.

items.prompt: Compare 5/9 and 3/8 by deciding whether each is greater than or less than 1/2. Write which fraction is greater and explain your steps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5/9 is greater than 1/2 because 2 × 5 = 10 > 9. 3/8 is less than 1/2 because 2 × 3 = 6 < 8. Since 5/9 is above 1/2 and 3/8 is below 1/2, we have 5/9 > 3/8.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For each fraction, double the numerator and compare with the denominator: if double the numerator exceeds the denominator the fraction is above 1/2; the fraction above 1/2 is greater.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: place both fractions on a number line with 0, 1/2, and 1 marked; stretch: choose a pair where both fractions are above 1/2 and ask the student to compare them.

items.prompt: Which symbol correctly fills the blank? 5/9 ___ 8/9

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5/9 < 8/9. Both fractions have the same denominator (9), so the one with the smaller numerator (5) is the smaller fraction.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: With the same denominator, compare numerators directly: the fraction with the smaller numerator is smaller.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student reversed the comparison, perhaps comparing denominators (both 9) and then choosing the larger of the two identical values, or misreading the numerators.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have focused on the equal denominators and concluded the fractions are equal, ignoring the different numerators.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not yet grasped that fractions with the same denominator can be compared directly by their numerators.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: draw a bar divided into 9 parts, shade 5 in one colour and then 8 in another, and compare visually; stretch: ask the student to order three fractions with denominator 9 from smallest to largest.

exercise.description: Compare fractions with same denominator using < and >: 1/4 & 3/4; 3/5 & 4/5; 5/7 & 2/7; 7/8 & 3/8; 5/10 & 6/10; 2/6 & 1/6.

items.prompt: Find the missing number: 3/5 = ?/20. Write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12. Multiply both numerator and denominator of 3/5 by 4 to get 12/20.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the factor by which the denominator was multiplied (5 × 4 = 20), then multiply the numerator by the same factor (3 × 4 = 12).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: draw a rectangle divided into 5 equal columns, shade 3, then divide each column into 4 rows to see the 20 parts; stretch: ask the student to find one more fraction equivalent to 3/5 using a different multiplying factor.

exercise.description: Fill boxes to make equivalent fractions: 2/5 = ?/10; 3/4 = ?/16; 4/7 = 8/?; 5/9 = ?/25.

items.prompt: A caterpillar is 1/3 cm long. If 12 caterpillars crawl in a straight line one after another, what is the total length of the line in cm? Use the number line to find your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 cm. Counting 12 steps of 1/3 gives 12/3, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Mark 12 steps of 1/3 on the number line, grouping every 3 steps into 1 whole; 12 steps give 4 wholes, so the total length is 4 cm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students: have them mark each 1/3 step one at a time and circle every group of three to make one whole; stretch: ask how long a line of 15 caterpillars would be if each is 1/3 cm.

exercise.description: If an ant is 1/4 cm long, find total length of 16 such ants in a line using the number line.
